sections.h2: What is Williamson County like for someone selling a house?
sections.html:
Williamson County sits in Southern Illinois, where Marion is the seat and also the biggest city. It was cut from Franklin County on February 28, 1839, and covers 444 square miles, of which 24 are water. The 2020 census counted 67,153 residents in 28,145 households, and homeowners lived in roughly 69% of the occupied units, with renters in the rest.

Coal mining shaped the county for more than a century, and the area still carries the "Bloody Williamson" nickname from that era. Cities include Marion, Herrin, Carterville, Johnston City, Creal Springs and Hurst, plus a slice of Carbondale. The county is divided into 12 congressional townships, and nine school districts serve it, among them Marion Community Unit School District 2, Herrin Community Unit School District 4 and Carterville Community Unit School District 5. Your bill reflects whichever district, city and township your parcel sits in.

Weather is a real factor for sellers in this county. The county was struck by two tornadoes on May 29, 1982, and Carterville, Herrin and Marion took heavy damage from the May 2009 derecho. Hail, wind and tornado repairs often turn up during a buyer's inspection, and the county has a property tax break aimed at rebuilt storm-damaged homes (covered below).

sections.h2: Which Williamson County offices handle the property tax bill?
sections.html:
Four offices touch the bill. Calling the right one saves a trip to the Administration Building at 407 N. Monroe Street in Marion.

  • The Supervisor of Assessments, Suite 205, keeps property records, takes exemption applications and runs the Board of Review paperwork. The office number is 618-998-2189.
  • The Board of Review rules on assessment complaints, and its clerk works out of the Supervisor's office.
  • The County Clerk files each taxing district's levy request and extends the tax to every parcel. Redemption after a tax sale also runs through the Clerk, at 618-998-2110.
  • The County Treasurer mails bills and collects. The counter is open weekdays from 8:00 am until 4:00 pm, and the phone is 618-998-2142.

The county's own summary of the cycle is simple: assessments are finished by the Supervisor and the Board of Review, the Clerk extends the tax, and then the Treasurer sends the bill. The Treasurer collects only. If a bill looks wrong, the question belongs with the assessment office, not the collector.

sections.h2: What are the Williamson County payment deadlines and options?
sections.html:
The Treasurer sends one bill a year with two installment due dates. The exact dates change with each tax year and are printed on the bill and posted on the Treasurer's collection schedule page, so read the stub for the current year before you plan a closing.

The county lists these ways to pay:

  • At most Williamson County banks, but only until the due date. After that, banks cannot collect and payment must be made at the Treasurer's office.
  • By mail, with an official U.S. postmark dated no later than the due date.
  • In person, including a night drop box.
  • Online with Visa, Mastercard, American Express, Discover or PayPal, or by phone at (618) 342-8470. The card company adds a convenience fee.

Enclose the installment stub so the right credit posts. Owners with several parcels can pay with one check if the parcel numbers are listed and each coupon is included. A canceled check serves as the receipt, or you can request an official one in writing. Where an escrow account covers the tax, the county still mails you a copy for your records.

sections.h2: How can an owner contest a Williamson County valuation?
sections.html:
The complaint goes to the Williamson County Board of Review and is due 30 days from publication of the assessment list by the Supervisor of Assessments. Missing that window usually ends the appeal for the year. The county FAQ says the only exception is wrong data that the value was built on, such as incorrect square footage.

The Board's 2025 rules set the practical details:

  • Complaint forms are available only at the Supervisor's office on North Monroe Street, or by first-class mail on request. Faxed or emailed forms are rejected.
  • Allowed grounds are overvaluation, equity, physical data discrepancy and preferential assessment. Complaints about the amount of tax, a rate change or a percentage jump do not qualify.
  • All evidence goes in on paper with the complaint. Late evidence and evidence in other formats is not considered.
  • Anyone who bought after January 1, 2022 must disclose the price, date and whether the sale was arm's length.
  • Hearings run in 15-minute slots, in person or by teleconference, and written findings are mailed within 10 business days.

Assessments equal one-third of fair cash value, measured on a January 1 valuation date from sales in the three prior years. Appraisals must come from a state-certified appraiser. Hearings on the 2025 complaints began April 9, 2026. The rules suggest talking with the Supervisor's office before filing, although the deadline stays put during those talks.

sections.h2: Which exemptions can lower a Williamson County tax bill?
sections.html:
Bring your tax statement to the Supervisor's office to apply. The county's notice describes the programs below.

Homestead programs the Williamson County assessment office takes applications for
ExemptionWho qualifiesAmount or note
Owner OccupiedResident owner as of the assessment-year start; no age requirementProof of ownership and photo ID required
Homestead (senior)Owner-occupant turning or already 65 in the assessment yearProof of age and residence required
Senior Citizen Assessment Freeze65 or older, in the home since the prior assessment year, household income under the capCap changes over time; confirm with the office
Homestead ImprovementOwner-occupied, residential use onlyAdded value up to $75,000; apply before October 7 or within 30 days of the publication, whichever comes later
Disabled Veterans' StandardService-connected rating of at least 30%$2,500 at 30% to 49%, $5,000 at 50% to 69%, tax exempt at 70% or more; annual filing
Returning VeteransVeteran home from active duty in an armed conflict$5,000 for two years
Disabled PersonsOwner who is 100% disabled, with proof$2,000; annual filing

A Natural Disaster Homestead Exemption also exists for a home rebuilt after storm, fire or flood damage. The structure must be rebuilt within two years, and the new square footage cannot exceed 110% of the original. Given the county's tornado history, this is worth a call if you are selling a house that was rebuilt.

sections.h2: What happens if Williamson County property tax goes unpaid?
sections.html:
Each missed due date starts a penalty of 1.5% per month, and delinquent bills pick up a $10 certified-mail and advertising cost. Tax still unpaid after the second installment date is delinquent and heads to the county's annual tax sale, held in December.

At the sale the investor who bids the lowest interest rate pays the Treasurer the taxes, costs and fees. The county sells the unpaid tax, not the house. Records then pass to the County Clerk, and the owner or anyone with a financial interest has from 6 months to 2 1/2 years from the sale to redeem. The buyer may extend that to as much as three years. Redemption takes a single full payment in certified funds payable to the Williamson County Clerk, in person or by mail.

The cost grows over time. The bid rate applies to one six-month period and repeats every six months. Later years' taxes can be added at 12% per year, and if the buyer starts the tax deed process, the court can be petitioned for a deed once redemption lapses. Call the Clerk with the parcel number to get a redemption estimate.

sections.h2: Who owes the tax when a Williamson County house sells?
sections.html:
The tax stays attached to the parcel, so an unpaid bill falls on the buyer unless the closing statement credits it. New owners are told to look for a seller credit on that statement or ask their attorney. Illinois bills a year behind, which means a sale in the fall usually leaves a bill for the year of sale still to come.

After a sale, sellers should forward any bill that arrives to the new owner, since the Treasurer accepts no responsibility for a payment applied to the wrong bill. A bill that never arrived still carries penalties. Before closing, have the closing agent verify that both installments of the latest bill are paid and that no earlier year sits with a tax buyer. Back taxes on your parcel mean a redemption estimate from the County Clerk comes first.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to appeal a Williamson County assessment?
faqs.a: Thirty days from publication of the assessment list. The Board rules say talks with the assessment office do not extend that period, so file first.

faqs.q: Can I pay Williamson County property tax by credit card?
faqs.a: Yes. Online payment accepts Visa, Mastercard, American Express, Discover and PayPal, and a phone option exists at (618) 342-8470. A convenience fee from the card company applies.

faqs.q: Does Williamson County sell my house at the tax sale?
faqs.a: No. The December tax sale sells the unpaid tax to an investor, not the property. The owner keeps the right to redeem for at least six months and up to 2 1/2 years, and the buyer may extend that to three years.

faqs.q: Which office fixes a missing exemption on a Williamson County bill?
faqs.a: The Supervisor of Assessments, at 618-998-2189. The county asks owners to look for owner-occupied and senior credits on the bill and to call that office when a qualifying credit is missing.

faqs.q: Who gets the tax bill after I sell in Williamson County?
faqs.a: The bill stays with the parcel. Settle it on the closing statement, get any seller credit in writing, and forward later bills to the new owner.
